To generate a maximal triangle-free graph with 14 vertices, we can use the concept of a complete bipartite graph. A complete bipartite graph is a graph whose vertices can be divided into two disjoint sets U and V such that every edge connects a vertex in U to one in V. In a complete bipartite graph, there are no triangles because there are no edges between vertices within the same set.

For a maximal triangle-free graph with 14 vertices, we can divide the vertices into two sets of 7 vertices each. This division ensures that the graph is triangle-free because there are no edges between vertices within the same set.

- Set U: \(v_0, v_1, ..., v_6\)
- Set V: \(v_7, v_8, ..., v_{13}\)

Every vertex in set U is connected to every vertex in set V. This gives us a complete bipartite graph \(K_{7,7}\), which is maximal triangle-free because adding any edge between vertices within the same set would create a triangle.

The edges of this graph can be listed as follows:
- \((v_0, v_7), (v_0, v_8), ..., (v_0, v_{13})\)

- ...

This results in a total of \(7 \times 7 = 49\) edges.
